assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 model of credit cycles shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a foundational mechanism in macro-finance and in the analysis of the financial crisis, and it shaped both research and policy thinking about balance-sheet channels.
assessment.attribution: The core contribution is clearly the Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles model, so a two-person award is clean. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the broader financial accelerator literature, which builds on work already recognised in 2022, so I leave them out of the proposed award.
assessment.maturity: About three decades of theory, quantitative extensions and empirical use have confirmed the mechanism. The timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises could be read as reducing novelty.
How to weigh the Kiyotaki-Moore contribution against the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist line is a judgement call.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: These authors formalised the study of how electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy outcomes, and they supported the formalisation with empirical tests. They created a coherent field of modern political economics that links institutions to economic outcomes. The field is close to my own, so I flag that proximity; I assess the work on the common criteria of originality, influence and verified results.
assessment.attribution: Persson-Tabellini (Political Economics, constitutions and fiscal outcomes) and Besley (state capacity, accountability) are the recognised principal figures. Three laureates fit the field's attribution, though the individual weighting is debatable.
assessment.maturity: More than 25 years of cumulative theoretical and empirical work, with wide uptake across economics and political science. Plenty of time has passed for validation.
uncertainties: Empirical identification in the constitutional-comparison studies has been challenged.
The 2024 institutions prize may make the committee reluctant to reward a neighbouring topic so soon.
Others, such as Acemoglu, are already recognised in this area, which complicates how to divide credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, Calvo and Taylor staggered pricing and contracting, and the Woodford-style New Keynesian framework are the working core of modern monetary policy analysis. They are used in central banks worldwide, and the Taylor rule is a standard guide to policy.
assessment.attribution: The list is crowded (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gali, Gertler, Smets also contribute). Calvo for time-dependent pricing, Taylor for contracts and the policy rule, and Woodford for the integrated framework are the clearest foundational roles, but others have strong claims.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. The framework has had decades of use, including stress tests in recent inflation episodes.
uncertainties: The three-laureate cap forces a difficult choice among strong contributors.
The framework's performance in the post-2021 inflation period and its relation to earlier laureates in monetary and macro theory are debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rubinstein's alternating-offers bargaining model gives non-cooperative foundations for bargaining outcomes, and Rubinstein-Wolinsky extend it to decentralised markets. The model underlies large literatures in game theory, labour and search economics and in applied models.
assessment.attribution: The 1982 Rubinstein model is the central contribution and the Rubinstein-Wolinsky market extension is the main follow-on. Binmore's contribution, on interpreting and connecting the model to the Nash solution, is real but less central, so I exclude him.
assessment.maturity: More than 40 years of acceptance as a standard tool. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Prior recognition of game theory (Nash, Harsanyi, Selten, Aumann, Myerson, and others) may reduce the committee's appetite for another game-theory award.
The reduced credit for Binmore may be seen as contentious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design provide a general framework for how a designer shapes the information others hold. The work links to mechanism design and global games and has applications in regulation, platforms, finance and disclosure.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica-Gentzkow originated Bayesian persuasion, while Bergemann and Morris developed the general information-design and robust-mechanism framework. Gentzkow's omission from a three-person cap is a significant attribution difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The core papers date from 2011 onwards, with substantial theory and a growing but still thinner empirical base.
uncertainties: It is unclear whether policy and empirical impact has yet matched the theoretical influence.
The three-person cap forces the exclusion of Gentzkow, and the proper division of credit is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Melitz's 2003 model of firm heterogeneity and selection reoriented international trade research, with Helpman and co-authors showing how exporting and productivity interact. It changed how welfare gains from trade and the effects of trade policy are measured and analysed.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 model is the principal contribution. Helpman is a broad contributor, with Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI. Redding's role is important in quantification and spatial extensions but is somewhat more derivative.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of extensive empirical validation and extension, and the framework is standard.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize on new trade theory may overlap in the committee's mind.
Helpman also appears in a separate political-economy trade entry, which could split support.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Manski's partial identification programme made explicit what can be learned from data under weak assumptions, and Tamer and Molinari extended it to practical inference. It addresses a basic problem in empirical economics: credible conclusions without implausible assumptions.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear founder. Tamer is a major developer, with sharp bounds in incomplete models. Molinari has strong inferential contributions but is more recent, so I propose only Manski and Tamer.
assessment.maturity: Manski's work is decades old and its influence on methodology and on thinking about credibility is clear. Applied uptake has been more limited than for other methods.
uncertainties: Applied adoption is narrower than that of the 2021 methodological laureates' work.
Whether the committee views this as a broad enough transformation of empirical practice is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based and skill-biased technical change framework and the evidence on trade shocks reshaped understanding of wage inequality and labour-demand change. The work has had major policy and scholarly influence on automation, trade and labour-market dislocation.
assessment.attribution: Autor's task-based and trade-shock work (with Dorn, Hanson) and Katz's long-standing work on skills and wages (with Goldin and Autor) are the central strands. Dorn and Hanson are credited for the China-shock results, so the cap makes attribution difficult. The prior prizes to Goldin (2023) and to Acemoglu (2024) may overlap.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature, with 20+ years of evidence, though the China-shock literature is still debated and updated.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes on labour markets, technology and inequality.
Empirical debate about the size and persistence of trade-shock effects.
The three-person cap excludes Dorn and Hanson.
